sections.heading: Seeing your goodness in everything you do
sections.text: Lord of heaven, your goodness is more than we can measure or fully understand. We see your power in everything you have made, your wisdom in the way you govern our lives, and your love most clearly in the good news of your grace. In your Son, you have given us everything we could never provide for ourselves: rescue from sin’s ruin, a right standing before you, hearts being made holy, and the promise that you will keep us on the road that leads to life.
theological_themes: God’s goodness is revealed in creation, providence, and the gospel.
Salvation in Christ includes deliverance, justification, sanctification, and perseverance.

scripture_references.connection: Paul praises God for the saving blessings given in Christ, including redemption, forgiveness, and God’s gracious purpose. This supports the prayer’s focus on the Father providing comprehensive salvation through the Son.
This passage holds together God’s saving work from his purpose to glorification. It grounds the prayer’s confidence that God not only begins salvation but carries his people through to the end.

sections.heading: Running to the refuge you have provided
sections.text: When your law shows us the truth about our guilt, we do not have to hide from you in despair. You have given us a shelter stronger than the storm. When we have to admit that we are unclean, you have opened a fountain that can wash sinners clean. When we come to you empty, needy, and unable to fill ourselves, we find in Christ a fullness that is open to us and never runs out.
theological_themes: God’s law exposes sin, but Christ provides refuge, cleansing, and fullness.
Human emptiness is answered by the inexhaustible sufficiency of Christ.

scripture_references.connection: Paul teaches that there is no condemnation for those in Christ because God has dealt with sin through his Son. This fits the prayer’s movement from the terror of the law to the refuge God gives in Christ.

John connects honest confession of sin with cleansing through Jesus’ blood and God’s faithfulness to forgive. This supports the prayer’s image of sinners being washed clean rather than pretending they are already pure.
Paul says the fullness of God dwells in Christ and that reconciliation comes through him. This grounds the prayer’s claim that our emptiness is met by an inexhaustible fullness in Jesus.

sections.heading: Letting Jesus become greater than everything else
sections.text: Teach us, again and again, that walking with Jesus changes the weight of everything else. Keep us from treating eternal things as an occasional interest, something we notice only when life slows down or trouble comes. Let knowing Christ make our lesser ambitions, comforts, and anxieties take their proper place, like shadows compared with what is real.
theological_themes: Fellowship with Christ relativizes earthly interests and reorders loves.
True discipleship requires steady attention to eternal realities, not occasional religious concern.

scripture_references.connection: Paul describes former gains as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ. This directly supports the prayer’s desire that life with Jesus make every competing interest secondary.
Paul calls believers to set their minds on things above because their life is hidden with Christ. This grounds the request to live with steady attention to eternal realities.

sections.heading: Protecting us from almost-Christianity
sections.text: Please save us from being satisfied with a faith that stops short of Christ himself. Keep us from being religiously interested but unchanged, stirred up but not born again, informed and confident but still without Jesus. Do not let us mistake excitement, strong opinions, spiritual language, or outward effort for the new life only you can give.
theological_themes: Religious concern, zeal, and knowledge can exist without true conversion.
Only God can give a new heart and true life in Christ.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus warns that outwardly impressive religious activity can exist without truly knowing him. This supports the prayer’s concern about confidence and zeal that do not have Christ at the center.
God promises to give his people a new heart and put his Spirit within them. This grounds the distinction between temporary religious feeling and the inward renewal that comes from God.

sections.heading: Testing whether our faith is real
sections.text: Help us examine our Christianity honestly. Let us not measure ourselves only by what we say we depend on, but also by whether we love Jesus, are becoming more like him, and truly know him. Make our trust more than a doctrine we can explain; make it a living bond with Christ that shows itself in love, obedience, humility, and desire for him.
theological_themes: True faith rests on Christ and is shown in love, conformity to him, and growing knowledge of him.
Self-examination should look for living union with Christ, not mere religious claims.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus teaches that abiding in him bears fruit and is inseparable from love and obedience. This supports the prayer’s desire for dependence on Christ that is visible in a changed life.
John gives knowledge of Christ a concrete test: keeping his commandments and walking as he walked. This supports the prayer’s call to judge faith by love for Christ and conformity to him.

sections.heading: Growing in a faith that keeps going
sections.text: Give us a faith that is real and keeps growing. Let it move forward instead of fading in and out. Let it live and work by the Holy Spirit. When you correct us, make us teachable and changed by it. And when sin offers us comfort, pleasure, or an easy excuse, do not let us make peace with it. Keep us close to Christ, stronger in grace, and faithful to the end.
theological_themes: Christian growth is progressive and Spirit-dependent.
God’s correction is meant to train believers in holiness.
Believers must not indulge the flesh but keep walking in the Spirit.

scripture_references.connection: Paul contrasts gratifying the flesh with walking by the Spirit and bearing the Spirit’s fruit. This directly supports the request for a faith that lives and works in the Spirit and is not damaged by sinful indulgence.
Hebrews presents the Lord’s discipline as the loving correction of a Father who trains his children in holiness. This grounds the prayer’s request to profit from every correction.
Paul expresses confidence that God will complete the good work he began in believers. This supports the prayer’s longing for persevering, strengthening, progressive faith.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original uses sharp distinctions between being merely religiously concerned and being truly converted. This can be pastorally sensitive, but it is central to the prayer and reflects biblical warnings about nominal or superficial faith.

The phrase about being exposed to the terrors of God’s law reflects a Reformed/Puritan law-gospel framework. The adaptation preserves the idea that the law exposes guilt while Christ provides refuge, without softening the warning.
significant_interpretive_choices: “Creature-cells of emptiness” was interpreted as describing human beings as finite, dependent, and empty in themselves before God. The modern version renders this as coming to God empty and unable to fill ourselves.

“Another heart but not a new one” was rendered as being stirred, interested, or outwardly changed without being born again. This preserves the original contrast between temporary religious alteration and genuine regeneration.

“Injured by no carnal indulgence” was not taken to mean that Christians can safely indulge sin, but that true, growing religion refuses to make peace with sinful indulgence and is kept from being corrupted by it.
